highlights.content: **2026-09-27(일)** [![Korea IT Times](/image/logo/toplogo_20260611110102.png)](https://www.koreaittimes.com) [![](/image/icon-en.png)English](https://www.koreaittimes.com/) [![](/image/icon-kr.png)KR](/index2.html?editcode=MAIN_9) * [Contact](/com/contact.html) * [Login](/member/login.html) * [Join](/member/index.html) * [Mobile](https://www.koreaittimes.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=157524) [![Korea IT Times](/image/logo/printlogo_20260611110102.png)](https://www.koreaittimes.com) KT AI Router Ranks No. 2 in Global Benchmark KT AI Router Ranks No. 2 in Global Benchmark * Jung So-yeon * Published 2026.09.27 15:59 * Comments [0](#reply) 이 기사를 공유합니다 --- AutoModelRouter balances AI performance and cost ![KT’s proprietary AI model routing technology, AutoModelRouter, ranked No. 2 overall in RouterArena, a public benchmark specializing in LLM routers / Courtesy of KT](/news/photo/202609/157524_107083_5932.jpg) KT’s proprietary AI model routing technology, AutoModelRouter, ranked No. 2 overall in RouterArena, a public benchmark specializing in LLM routers / Courtesy of KT KT said its proprietary AI model routing technology, AutoModelRouter, ranked second in the Acc-Cost Arena of RouterArena, a global benchmark for evaluating large language model (LLM) routers. RouterArena was developed by researchers at Rice University in the United States. The research was accepted as a regular paper at ICLR 2026, an international machine learning conference. The platform evaluates AI routers using about 8,400 queries, measuring response accuracy, cost efficiency and robustness to changes in input. KT’s technology is listed on the RouterArena public leaderboard as “KT-ModelRouter.” It ranked No. 2 in the Acc-Cost Arena, which evaluates both response quality and cost efficiency. The leaderboard includes technologies developed by academic researchers as well as commercial solutions such as Microsoft’s Azure Model Router. The result highlights KT’s efforts to strengthen its AI orchestration capabilities as enterprises increasingly adopt multiple AI models. Rather than relying on a single model for all tasks, companies are adopting multi-model environments because each AI model has different strengths, performance levels and pricing. For example, relatively simple tasks such as translation or information searches can be handled by cost-efficient models, while complex analysis and advanced reasoning may require higher-performance models. AutoModelRouter analyzes a user’s request based on factors including task type, difficulty and knowledge domain. It then selects an appropriate AI model by considering the quality and cost of each model. The system does not simply select the highest-performing or cheapest model. Instead, it is designed to meet the required quality level while improving cost efficiency. A lower-cost model can be assigned to simple translation or information-checking tasks, while a high-performance model can handle complex document analysis or advanced reasoning. From the user’s perspective, the process takes place within a single AI service. Behind the scenes, however, different AI models can be deployed depending on the characteristics of each request. The technology could become increasingly important as companies expand the use of generative AI across business operations. As AI usage grows, companies also face rising token costs, making efficient allocation of AI models an important part of managing enterprise AI spending. Model routing can also reduce the burden on companies of comparing newly released AI models based on performance, pricing and suitability for different applications. A flexible routing system allows companies to add or replace models while managing performance and costs across a multi-model environment. He said the massive AI training supercomputer could double the number of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) deployed by year-end. In the post, Musk noted that Colossus 2 currently has 110,000 Nvidia GB200 chips and 440,000 GB300s. An additional 220,000 GB300 chips are set to come online next week, with another 220,000 GPUs set for November. He added that he hopes to get another 220,000 GB300s in late December, "if we get lucky." highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [AI & Machine Learning](https://shattered.io/ai-machine-learning/) # MiniCPM5-2B Beats Bigger Rivals by 2.8 Points [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/panand.webp) [Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/author/panand/) Updated Sep 27, 2026 · 13 min read A 2.5-billion-parameter language model just beat a 4-billion-parameter rival on a 34-benchmark test suite, and the gap that matters fits in two numbers: 53.9 versus 51.1. OpenBMB released MiniCPM5-2B in September 2026, and its model card claims the small model reaches open-source state of the art at the 2B parameter class while topping every larger model in its own comparison table. That is not a rounding error. It is the latest data point in a shift that has been building quietly for a year and is now hard to miss: small AI models are closing the gap with systems many times their size, and the fallout reaches from phone battery life to GPU order books. ## A Crowded Week for Small AI Model Releases MiniCPM5-2B did not land alone. Between September 25 and September 27, 2026, MarkTechPost’s machine learning desk logged a cluster of small-model releases that, taken together, read like a coordinated bet against the “bigger is always better” era of large language models. Liquid AI shipped LFM2.5-VL-3B-DSpark, a 279.5-million-parameter draft model built to speed up its LFM2.5-VL-3B vision-language model through speculative decoding. Supersonic Labs put out Julia 1, a 144.3-million-parameter decision model built on mmBERT-small. Sarvam AI released Saaras V4, a speech-to-text model covering all 22 official Indian languages plus global English. And Ornith AI pushed out Ornith-1.5-9B, a 9-billion-parameter model that Hermes AI reported performing close to 35-billion-parameter models on reasoning tasks. None of these labs are household names outside AI research circles. That is part of the story. The frontier-model race between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google still dominates headlines, but a second race is running underneath it, and it is about squeezing more capability out of fewer parameters rather than adding more of them. ## What Is MiniCPM5-2B, and Why It Stands Out MiniCPM5-2B is a dense causal language model, meaning it generates text token by token rather than routing through a mixture-of-experts architecture. According to its [Hugging Face model card](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B), the model carries 2,516,756,480 parameters and supports a native context window of 131,072 tokens, enough to hold a mid-sized codebase or a lengthy legal contract in a single pass. OpenBMB, the lab behind the MiniCPM series, has built its reputation on exactly this kind of efficiency-first design rather than chasing raw parameter counts. The model’s [GitHub repository](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenBMB/MiniCPM/main/README.md) repeats the same benchmark claim found on the model card, and it is worth being precise about what is actually being measured. OpenBMB tested MiniCPM5-2B against a set of larger open-source models across 34 benchmarks spanning coding, math, instruction following, general knowledge, long-context understanding, tool use, and agentic tasks. Within that specific comparison set, MiniCPM5-2B came out on top. ## The Benchmark Math: 53.9 vs. 51.1 The headline figure is a 53.9 average score for MiniCPM5-2B against a 51.1 average for the strongest model in OpenBMB’s comparison set, commonly cited in coverage as Qwen3.5-4B. A 2.8-point margin sounds modest until you remember the size difference: MiniCPM5-2B is roughly 1.6 times smaller in parameter count than the model it edged out. Smaller weights mean less memory, faster inference, and cheaper hosting, so a 2.8-point win at half the footprint is a meaningfully different trade than a 2.8-point win between two similarly sized models. highlights.content: # Cheap tokens fuel AI usage surge, pushing task costs higher Falling token rates mask pricier AI tasks as agents and reasoning swell usage By  [Kim Su-jeong](https://biz.chosun.com/en/people/kim-sujeong/) Published 2026.09.28. 06:00 [Prefer Chosunbiz EN on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=biz.chosun.com) The token price paid for using artificial intelligence (AI) models has fallen to an all-time low. The rise of low-cost Chinese models and intensifying price competition among global AI corporations are to blame. But as high-performance reasoning models and AI agents consume more tokens in the course of doing tasks, a paradox has emerged in which actual usage expense is increasing. Analysts say the benchmark for gauging the cost competitiveness of AI models is shifting from simple "price per token" to the "expense per task," the cost to complete a single real-world task. Graphic = Son Min-gyun On the 28th, market research firm SiliconData said its "large language model (LLM) token spending index" fell to 97 cents on the 31st of the last month (local time). That is the lowest since the index was released late last year and less than half of the peak recorded this summer. The LLM token spending index is not a simple per-vendor unit price; it measures the weighted average price per 1 million tokens actually consumed in the market. It normalizes weights daily, reflecting each model's input/output token shares and usage. The drop in token prices has been driven by low-price offensives from Chinese AI firms. As Chinese open-source models such as Kimi expanded their influence by leveraging low prices, global AI corporations also moved to cut prices in succession. The article examines how a new generation of AI systems can connect functions and reduce the coordination friction that slows companies down, citing Xsight’s practice of decomposing complex cross-departmental decisions into modular tasks and building a layered agentic AI orchestration system as a valuable model for cross-border organizational coordination. **The Hidden Bottleneck in Cross-Functional Decision-Making** The HBR article opens with a tariff scenario that many global organizations will recognize: a CEO directs the company to pull forward inventory before a new tariff takes effect, yet weeks later the strategy remains unexecuted. After rounds of revisions and compromises among procurement, logistics, finance, legal, marketing, sales and merchandising, the company implements a patchwork of suboptimal actions. The article argues that such breakdowns are not caused by bureaucracy or risk aversion, but by a basic limitation: “No single individual’s brain can hold all the relevant information, constraints, and scenarios.” Information is asymmetric, and issues and risks emerge one by one rather than all at once. Delays in executing cross-functional strategies, the authors argue, are “signals that the organization has exceeded its capacity to orchestrate decisions.” Even companies with task-based AI tools are still struggling, because most agents operate independently within functions. As the article notes, when specialized agents operate independently, “their outputs may conflict.” **Xsight Group’s Approach: Modular Decisions and Layered AI Orchestration** The HBR article identifies Xsight as one of two companies studied that achieved significant improvement in orchestration by dividing decisions into precise, well-defined tasks. This means specifying inputs, outputs, constraints and objectives of each task and standardizing information and assumptions so that procurement, logistics and finance all work from the same definitions. With this as the basis, Xsight developed a multi-layered agentic AI orchestration system. At the task level, specialized AI agents handle contract analysis, demand forecasting and capacity planning. At the orchestration level, connectors verify that outputs stay within management-specified guardrails and route validated information across workflows, while a master AI orchestrator structures and coordinates the analyses and human input needed for enterprise decisions. “This system is not designed to replace management in making final business decisions. Illustration/Aktualita.co **Jakarta, Aktualita.co —** The development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology entered a new chapter in 2026. While a few years ago AI was synonymous with chatbots that received questions and generated text, the technology is now evolving into **[AI agents](https://aktualita.co/teknologi/agen-ai-openai-akses-portal-medicare-australia-tanpa-izin-keamanan-ai-otonom-jadi-sorotan)** capable of executing a series of tasks more independently. This shift is evident in the technological advancements introduced by major companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. AI capabilities are no longer limited to writing, translating, or creating images; they now encompass software usage, browser operation, video analysis, real-time voice processing, and the completion of long-running tasks. This phenomenon has shifted the AI competition away from simply determining which model is the smartest. The race has moved toward an AI system's ability to **perform real-world work using various digital tools**. ## AI Evolves from Chatbot to Agent A significant development occurred when OpenAI introduced the Agents API on September 10, 2026. This technology allows developers to build cloud-based agents that can manage context, utilize various tools, execute code, work with files, and coordinate multiple sub-agents. OpenAI explained that useful agents require an infrastructure capable of maintaining context while executing tasks stably over long periods. This change demonstrates how AI is evolving from a conversation-based system into a digital work tool. Imagine a user asking an AI to analyze hundreds of documents, compare data, run code, and then compile a report. In previous generations, most of this process had to be done through many separate instructions. AI agents are designed to manage those work stages more automatically. Google is also moving in a similar direction. The company has introduced various agent-based experiences through the Gemini ecosystem, including the ability to use computers and perform actions on browsers, mobile devices, and desktop environments. ## More Natural Voice AI AI advancements in 2026 are also occurring in voice technology. In September, Google introduced Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking. These models are designed to conduct near [real-time](https://aktualita.co/teknologi/indosat-huawei-penerjemah-ai-real-time-telepon-beda-bahasa) conversations while handling more complex reasoning. This technology does not just listen to voices. The system can also understand visual context and perform tasks using tools in the background while a conversation is still ongoing. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [AI & Machine Learning](https://shattered.io/ai-machine-learning/) # MiniCPM5-2B Beats Bigger Rivals by 2.8 Points [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/panand.webp) [Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/author/panand/) Updated Sep 27, 2026 · 13 min read A 2.5-billion-parameter language model just beat a 4-billion-parameter rival on a 34-benchmark test suite, and the gap that matters fits in two numbers: 53.9 versus 51.1. OpenBMB released MiniCPM5-2B in September 2026, and its model card claims the small model reaches open-source state of the art at the 2B parameter class while topping every larger model in its own comparison table. That is not a rounding error. It is the latest data point in a shift that has been building quietly for a year and is now hard to miss: small AI models are closing the gap with systems many times their size, and the fallout reaches from phone battery life to GPU order books. ## A Crowded Week for Small AI Model Releases MiniCPM5-2B did not land alone. Between September 25 and September 27, 2026, MarkTechPost’s machine learning desk logged a cluster of small-model releases that, taken together, read like a coordinated bet against the “bigger is always better” era of large language models. Liquid AI shipped LFM2.5-VL-3B-DSpark, a 279.5-million-parameter draft model built to speed up its LFM2.5-VL-3B vision-language model through speculative decoding. Supersonic Labs put out Julia 1, a 144.3-million-parameter decision model built on mmBERT-small. Sarvam AI released Saaras V4, a speech-to-text model covering all 22 official Indian languages plus global English. And Ornith AI pushed out Ornith-1.5-9B, a 9-billion-parameter model that Hermes AI reported performing close to 35-billion-parameter models on reasoning tasks. None of these labs are household names outside AI research circles. That is part of the story. The frontier-model race between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google still dominates headlines, but a second race is running underneath it, and it is about squeezing more capability out of fewer parameters rather than adding more of them. ## What Is MiniCPM5-2B, and Why It Stands Out MiniCPM5-2B is a dense causal language model, meaning it generates text token by token rather than routing through a mixture-of-experts architecture. According to its [Hugging Face model card](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B), the model carries 2,516,756,480 parameters and supports a native context window of 131,072 tokens, enough to hold a mid-sized codebase or a lengthy legal contract in a single pass. OpenBMB, the lab behind the MiniCPM series, has built its reputation on exactly this kind of efficiency-first design rather than chasing raw parameter counts. The model’s [GitHub repository](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenBMB/MiniCPM/main/README.md) repeats the same benchmark claim found on the model card, and it is worth being precise about what is actually being measured. OpenBMB tested MiniCPM5-2B against a set of larger open-source models across 34 benchmarks spanning coding, math, instruction following, general knowledge, long-context understanding, tool use, and agentic tasks. Within that specific comparison set, MiniCPM5-2B came out on top. ## The Benchmark Math: 53.9 vs. 51.1 The headline figure is a 53.9 average score for MiniCPM5-2B against a 51.1 average for the strongest model in OpenBMB’s comparison set, commonly cited in coverage as Qwen3.5-4B. A 2.8-point margin sounds modest until you remember the size difference: MiniCPM5-2B is roughly 1.6 times smaller in parameter count than the model it edged out. Smaller weights mean less memory, faster inference, and cheaper hosting, so a 2.8-point win at half the footprint is a meaningfully different trade than a 2.8-point win between two similarly sized models. LLMs.titleZh: Cheap tokens fuel AI usage surge, pushing task costs higher
LLMs.content: # Cheap tokens fuel AI usage surge, pushing task costs higher Falling token rates mask pricier AI tasks as agents and reasoning swell usage By  [Kim Su-jeong](https://biz.chosun.com/en/people/kim-sujeong/) Published 2026.09.28. 06:00 [Prefer Chosunbiz EN on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=biz.chosun.com) The token price paid for using artificial intelligence (AI) models has fallen to an all-time low. The rise of low-cost Chinese models and intensifying price competition among global AI corporations are to blame. But as high-performance reasoning models and AI agents consume more tokens in the course of doing tasks, a paradox has emerged in which actual usage expense is increasing. Analysts say the benchmark for gauging the cost competitiveness of AI models is shifting from simple "price per token" to the "expense per task," the cost to complete a single real-world task. Graphic = Son Min-gyun On the 28th, market research firm SiliconData said its "large language model (LLM) token spending index" fell to 97 cents on the 31st of the last month (local time). That is the lowest since the index was released late last year and less than half of the peak recorded this summer. The LLM token spending index is not a simple per-vendor unit price; it measures the weighted average price per 1 million tokens actually consumed in the market. It normalizes weights daily, reflecting each model's input/output token shares and usage. The drop in token prices has been driven by low-price offensives from Chinese AI firms. As Chinese open-source models such as Kimi expanded their influence by leveraging low prices, global AI corporations also moved to cut prices in succession. OpenAI in July cut the API prices of GPT-5.6 "Tera" and "Luna" by 20% and 80%, respectively, and in August lowered the price of "Sol" by 20% as well. Google last month launched "Gemini 3.7 Flash" at $0.75 per 1 million input tokens and $3.75 per 1 million output tokens, about half the level of the previous model. As the performance gap between Chinese models and frontier models has narrowed, price competition in the AI industry has become more intense. However, observers note that lower token prices do not automatically translate into reduced AI usage expense. Recently, high-performance AI models go through longer chains of reasoning to solve complex problems, and autonomous AI agents repeat numerous model calls and verifications in the course of carrying out a single task. Thus, even if the per-token price falls, actual expense can increase if usage jumps sharply. In the end, actual AI expense is determined by token usage as well as the per-token price. Anthropic's latest model, "Claude Fable 5.1," is a representative case. While keeping Fable 5.1's input/output prices at the existing $10 and $50 per 1 million tokens, Anthropic lowered the cache read price by 75%, from $1 to $0.25. But on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (AAII), the expense per task under the Maximum effort standard was $3.69, 18% higher than the previous model Fable 5's $3.14. That is because to deliver higher performance, Fable 5.1 used about 1.7 times more output tokens than the previous model. Actual data also show diverging trends in token prices and usage. Google said in May that monthly token throughput had risen sevenfold in a year to 3,200 trillion, and the U.S. business magazine Fortune reported that although token prices have fallen by more than 90% since 2023, overall LLM expenditure has roughly doubled since late last year. The per-token price has dropped, but as usage growth outpaces it, total expense can actually become larger. The Economist in June also cited an analysis by Georgia Tech researcher Du Zheng, reporting that in the same task one DeepSeek model used about 23 times more tokens than an OpenAI competitor model. It said the cost competitiveness of models should therefore be judged not by simple price per token but by how many tokens and how much expense ...

KT announced that its self-developed AI model routing technology, AutoModelRouter, ranked second overall in RouterArena, a specialized public benchmark for large language model routers. RouterArena is an evaluation platform developed by researchers at Rice University in the United States, and it has gained enough credibility to be accepted as an official paper at ICLR 2026, an international conference on machine learning. Through approximately 8,400 queries, it comprehensively measures actual service operation performance, including the response accuracy, cost efficiency, and robustness to input variations of AI routers. KT placed at the top of the rankings in the Acc-Cost Arena criterion, which evaluates both accuracy and cost, surpassing commercial technologies such as Microsoft Azure Model Router. When a user request is received, AutoModelRouter immediately analyzes the task type, difficulty, and knowledge domain. It then connects the most suitable AI model according to pre-configured policies regarding response quality and usage cost for each model. Instead of processing all tasks with high-cost, high-performance models, it maximizes efficiency by assigning highly cost-effective models for simple translations or information verification, and deploying high-performance models only in areas requiring specialized reasoning. Enterprise customers can alleviate the inconvenience of having to manually compare and select numerous AI models through this technology. In particular, its ability to flexibly configure the AI operating environment according to the required level and budget for each task is considered a major strength. While users feel as though they are using a single service, the actual internal system operates in a structure where different optimal models are driven based on the characteristics of the request. KT is also applying this technology to the model routing function of its Token Factory. In the process of Token Factory operating various AI models and token usage environments in an integrated manner, AutoModelRouter will play the role of a core engine optimizing quality and cost. The company plans to establish a multi-model operating environment where new AI models can be flexibly added in the future, aiming to support the AI transformation of enterprises in all directions. Kim Jun-seok, Vice President and Head of the Agentic AI Lab at KT, explained, “In the AI era, orchestration capability to intelligently utilize models suitable for the situation is as important as securing an outstanding single model,” adding, “AutoModelRouter will be the core technology supporting KT’s competitive edge in agentic AI services.” **Shin So-hyeon** [pr@businesskorea.co.kr](mailto:pr@businesskorea.co.kr) [View More Article](/news/articleList.html?sc_area=I&sc_word=bktoday981&view_type=sm) Copyright © BusinessKorea. EVREN serves a broad range of users, from defence industry firms and technology companies to academics, entrepreneurs and students, bringing data, AI models and high-performance computing power together on a single platform, according to a statement from the Presidency of Defence Industries on Sunday. Prompt, response and usage data on the platform are processed on high-performance GPU infrastructure located in Türkiye, preventing sensitive data from being transferred to cloud services abroad. It can be accessed at [evren.ssyz.org.tr](https://evren.ssyz.org.tr/) using e-Government authentication. [![](https://d341l694dl30ad.cloudfront.net/images/cms/2026/08/18/6a842a07a3d67535e8261a16/original/8e6fe0dd-b270-4b85-8a0d-dc9cf0dbe845-1787046407122.webp?width=1080&format=jpg&quality=80) Related**TRT World - Türkiye launches 2026-2030 roadmap to become global AI hub**](https://www.trtworld.com/article/cd19ce1c04bd) **Contribute, earn credits, use GPU power** EVREN operates through a contribution-based credit model rather than direct paid access. Users can earn credits by uploading datasets, labeling data or sharing their trained models. The credits can be used for model training and large language model (LLM) inference operations through the platform's high-performance GPU pool. The system aims to make users active participants who contribute to the development of the EVREN ecosystem rather than merely receiving services. AI Product.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Alibaba Cloud VP Huo Jia: Enterprise AI failures mostly stem from picking the wrong use case; betting on results-based pricing [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Alibaba Cloud Intelligence Group Vice President Huo Jia said at the 2026 Apsara Conference that the real reason enterprise AI deployments fail is not insufficient model capability, but picking the wrong use case, overestimating the quality of one's own data, and applying traditional IT project methods to AI. AI Product.content: This is an as-told-to conversation with Daniel Dantus, a former BCG partner who's now a senior vice president at Skan AI, a startup that analyzes how work happens across a company. This conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity. I came into consulting as an undergraduate at the University of Michigan's business school. I joined a student consulting club and landed at Boston Consulting Group in Chicago, first as an intern, and then full time. What was special about BCG was that you were given a lot of rope from day one. My first week was training. By the second, I was on a manufacturing floor working with a large food-and-beverage company. We flew to Dallas and Mexico and visited plants. I was 20 years old. I was learning to enter new environments, build relationships, and have an impact. I was at BCG for a total of eight years. For the first six, every project involved a different client, city, and team. Firms recommend continuity, but I loved diving into new things. I did operations work in manufacturing and supply chain, as well as in financial services. Later, after I moved to San Francisco, I worked in tech, focusing on sales and product strategy. When I was promoted to project leader, my work shifted from delivering work to figuring out where I was going to build a business. I realized I wanted to keep learning and building products, which consulting projects generally do not allow over the long term. So I took some transition time from the firm, which is paid time to take a breather and find the next thing. I made a list of companies I thought might be interesting and people I knew who might be worth talking to. I had about 100 conversations. Job searches are a numbers game, like sales. If you want to sell to 10 customers, you'd better start talking to 200. That process led me to Harbor Freight Tools, a tool and equipment retailer, as the Director of Marketing, right after BCG. The mandate was to build out the company's digital marketing capability. It was my first "real job" after consulting, and I wasn't sure how learning to build PowerPoints would translate into delivering results. Still, by launching and scaling HFT's digital marketing channels across search, social, and display, I learned it did. Two years later, I ended up at Juul. I had worked with the head of corporate strategy on a BCG project when he worked at Constellation Brands. He later went to Juul to build a new capability. I reached out to catch up, and it happened to be good timing. I started working on its corporate strategy team, then later ran global travel retail and product. It was a turbulent time for the company. We went from about 1,000 employees to about 4,000 and then back to 1,000. It was also the first time I got to run a business over a longer term. Travel retail was my first sales job. You learn what it is like to be told no, to negotiate hard, to develop relationships, and to stand your ground. In my final two years, I ran product and e-liquid development, my first technical role alongside a business role. I learned how to take a product to market. I later returned to BCG as a partner. My work consisted of serving private equity clients in strategic due diligence. My advice to people leaving consulting is that no single job is that important. Take time to pause and reflect, and do outreach in addition to considering inbound opportunities. If a job does not work out the way you thought, you can always get another one. Traditional C2 detection tools cannot see it. [◆ Heath Callahan](https://forkast.news/minds/heath_forkast/)Forkast mind| CARBONATO is a Docker-based botnet that utilizes an autonomous AI agent as its command-and-control (C2) engine rather than a static server. Discovered by [ThreatDown](https://www.threatdown.com/blog/carbonato/) researchers in August 2026, this is the first documented instance where the C2 infrastructure reasons through its environment to adapt to the specific configuration of each compromised host, moving beyond the hardcoded scripts typical of traditional botnets. The technical implementation is deceptively simple. The implant deploys the [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent), an open-source framework from Nous Research released under the MIT license, without modifying the underlying binary. Instead, the operators overwrite the SOUL.md persona file with a 39-line prompt. This prompt renames the agent GH0ST and provides the operational instructions: maintain persistence, respond to Telegram commands, and prioritize the collection of credentials. When an operator issues a task via Telegram, the agent forwards the request along with the SOUL.md instructions to an LLM gateway. The model then generates terminal commands, interprets the output, and determines the subsequent steps, effectively automating the reconnaissance and exploitation process. This architecture creates a self-funding loop that distinguishes CARBONATO from its predecessors. The botnet prioritizes the theft of AI API keys above all other data, including SSH credentials and databases. The 39-line prompt names 14 providers explicitly: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Gemini, OpenRouter, Together, Groq, Mistral, Cohere, LocalAI, Ollama, vLLM, LiteLLM, and One API. These stolen keys are used to power the operators’ own LLM gateway, which was observed live on September 3, 2026, advertising 12 models and serving 27 through its API on a free tier. By leveraging stolen resources to fund the infrastructure that drives the botnet, the operators have created a sustainable model for offensive operations. The agent’s output is non-deterministic, meaning it reasons through the data it finds on each host, allowing it to tailor its approach to the system’s specific configuration. Traditional defensive tools designed to detect fixed-pattern C2 traffic are largely ineffective against CARBONATO. Because the malicious behavior is driven by loaded instructions rather than the binary itself, there is no static signature to block. The botnet’s spreading mechanism remains non-AI — scanning connected networks and Docker bridges for exposed daemons on port 2375 every five minutes — but the post-exploitation activity is entirely fluid. The Beijing-based lab published Kimi K3 as an open-weight model in July 2026, but it is only now, with Amazon Bedrock listing the model on September 18 and Unsloth shipping an updated deployment guide on September 8, that Kimi K3 is becoming something enterprise teams outside China can actually run in production. TechJuice was among the first outlets to break down the model’s architecture, and the specs it described are still the numbers everyone in the open-weight community is arguing about. At the center of the story is a single, striking figure: 1.56 terabytes. That is the size of the Kimi K3 checkpoint sitting on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3), split across 96 safetensors shards. It is one of the largest open-weight model releases to date, and it is forcing a fresh round of questions about what “open weights” even means when a single download is bigger than most people’s home internet connections can handle in a day. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. According to the official [GitHub repository](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/Kimi-K3) and Hugging Face model card, Moonshot AI describes it as “our most capable model: a 2.8T MoE model with native visual understanding and a 1M-token context window.” That single sentence packs in most of the headline specs journalists have been repeating since the release: 2.8 trillion total parameters, native multimodal input, and a context window that stretches past one million tokens. Moonshot AI’s documentation puts the activated parameter count at 104 billion per token, routed through 896 total experts of which 16 are selected per forward pass, plus two shared experts that process every token regardless of routing. That sparse-activation design is what makes a 2.8-trillion-parameter model computationally closer to a 100-billion-parameter dense model in practice, at least for inference cost, even though the full weight set still has to be stored and, in most deployment scenarios, loaded into memory. Open Source AI.title: Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money
Open Source AI.titleZh: Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money
Open Source AI.content: Big AI has a problem. Its companies must ingest other people’s work. You know, books, news stories, photographs, code, websites, that one original meme you came up with, and practically everything else on the internet to train its large language models (LLMs). We all know that. We also know that AI companies hate paying for any of it, obeying the licenses attached to it, or, God forbid, sharing their revenue with the companies and people who created the work in the first place. Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, was quoted in the news plaintiffs' 92-page combined brief as saying: the case was about “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Indeed, it waspossibly the “largest theft of labor in human history,” he was quoted as saying in the summary judgment brief from the journalists' lawyers [PDF].This, mind you, wasn't a comment by a member of the press; it was from a senior Microsoft staffer. REG AD Hecht wasn't the only one at Microsoft who commented. In an internal Microsoft policy document also quoted in the court papers, the authors admitted generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained [because] LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.” That, in turn, leads to model collapse. Ironically, AI is killing the content-creator goose that lays the gold eggs of worthwhile content. REG AD Judge Sidney H. Stein of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York has not yet issued a decision on the case. OpenAI and Microsoft are actively disputing the plaintiffs' allegations under a "fair use" defense. They contend that using public articles and books to train large language models helps push forward public knowledge, and isn't acting as a "unlawful economic market substitute". But the statements the documents cites are real. Big AI knows it needs the content. Some of the companies concerned don't give a damn; money now, worry later is their motto. Those who can look past the revenue numbers are well aware they're engaged in what Microsoft itself called a “doom loop” of AI content strategy in those unsealed court documents. Will that stop them? Nah. According to the filing [PDF], which refers to sworn deposition testimony of OpenAI’s own corporate representative, it also testified that its LLMs were happy to vacuum up other people's work even when a paywall nominally protected it. Its rep was quoted as saying they were unaware of “any effort to detect paywall content in its training datasets” or “to remove paywall content from its training datasets.” When OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman was told OpenAI could hack its way through the firewall, he responded, “ah, nice.” Whether or not these statements are found to be reflective of a wider attitude, similar attitudes prevail amongst Big AI. Such policies could eventually come back and bite the LLM makers; it's already affecting the market for journalism, fiction writing, graphics creation, anything that demands humans actually get paid for producing original work. But Big AI just doesn't want to pay for it.That's not a side effect. It's the business model. Joe User couldn't care less. They just want a quick answer that sounds right. Some of them couldn't care less about getting the right answers.As for looking deeper to see if the information they're regurgitating is accurate, forget about it! As an OpenAI software engineer put it: “No matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.” Well, I click. That's a big reason why Perplexity is my AI of choice. It's not that it gives a more reliable answer. No, it's that, unlike most LLMs, Perplexity provides sources and links, and I check them before accepting what it tells me. But then I'm a journalist whose degrees are in history, where my professors drummed into me that you always - always - look at the primary sources. Open Source AI.content: [Kingy AI](https://kingy.ai/) Explore Search Kingy AI [Work with Kingy](https://kingy.ai/for-ai-companies/) Menu AI News # GitHub’s New AI Fuzzing Taskflow: How It Works and Where It Can Go Wrong September 27, 2026 [Curtis Pyke](https://kingy.ai/curtis-pyke/) [AI News](https://kingy.ai/category/news/) GitHub Security Lab has published an open-source fuzzing taskflow for C and C++ projects. It asks an AI agent to find promising entry points, write test harnesses, run AFL++, examine coverage gaps, and triage crashes. The useful advance is a loop around coverage: the agent can decide what to change when a fuzzer stops reaching new code. The sharp limit is equally clear in GitHub’s own account: the workflow runs compiler and build commands chosen by the model on its host, and its vulnerability verdicts and suggested fixes require human review. [GitHub Security Lab’s technical article](https://github.blog/security/application-security/ai-powered-fuzzing-with-the-github-security-lab-taskflow-agent/) · [public repository](https://github.com/GitHubSecurityLab/seclab-taskflows-fuzzing) GitHub published the walkthrough on September 24, 2026. This article is based on GitHub’s explanation and source repository, checked September 27. Kingy did not run a campaign, validate a vulnerability, or measure its success rate. ## Why a fuzzing agent is useful A conventional fuzzer mutates inputs and watches for crashes. It does not know which untested API deserves a new harness or whether a flat coverage line means the inputs are poor, the harness is too narrow, or the unreachable path is irrelevant. A person typically reads coverage reports, writes harnesses, adjusts seeds and dictionaries, and investigates crashes. GitHub’s taskflow delegates much of that repeated work to an agent while using established fuzzing tools for execution. [GitHub technical article](https://github.blog/security/application-security/ai-powered-fuzzing-with-the-github-security-lab-taskflow-agent/) The pipeline has three layers: a shell driver, YAML taskflows that describe stages, and MCP tools for operations such as compiling a harness, running AFL and storing crash data. GitHub says the agent makes decisions while the tools perform the actions. State passes between stages through a SQLite database. This is a specific design, not a claim that the model can safely execute arbitrary security research on its own. [GitHub technical article](https://github.blog/security/application-security/ai-powered-fuzzing-with-the-github-security-lab-taskflow-agent/) ## The coverage loop, in plain language For each generated harness, the taskflow builds two binaries. One includes AFL instrumentation and sanitizers for fuzzing. The other includes coverage instrumentation so recorded inputs can be replayed to reveal source lines and branches reached. The agent reads uncovered branches and chooses whether to add a seed, widen a harness, enrich a dictionary, or leave an unpromising path alone. [GitHub technical article](https://github.blog/security/application-security/ai-powered-fuzzing-with-the-github-security-lab-taskflow-agent/) GitHub’s example doubles the fuzzing time budget through rounds of 30, 60, 120, 240, 480 and 960 seconds, approximately 32 minutes per target in total. Its default plateau rule stops after two rounds each improving absolute line coverage by less than one percentage point. Those are implementation defaults described by the project, not proof that 32 minutes is enough to find a bug or that one percentage point is the right threshold for every codebase. [GitHub technical article](https://github.blog/security/application-security/ai-powered-fuzzing-with-the-github-security-lab-taskflow-agent/) The pipeline can seed structured inputs using dictionaries and mutators for formats including JSON, XML, regular expressions, PNG and length-prefixed binary data. The rise of low-cost Chinese models and intensifying price competition among global AI corporations are to blame. But as high-performance reasoning models and AI agents consume more tokens in the course of doing tasks, a paradox has emerged in which actual usage expense is increasing. Analysts say the benchmark for gauging the cost competitiveness of AI models is shifting from simple "price per token" to the "expense per task," the cost to complete a single real-world task. ![Image 3: Graphic = Son Min-gyun](https://biz.chosun.com/resizer/v2/6TXNXHGSENGG3OMIJ7VNWPP5IY.jpg?auth=0a838fccbf6bc7b19a1360fd2b2ae18b7c0bdcff82f4a145ac47f5c0497579a6&width=616) Graphic = Son Min-gyun On the 28th, market research firm SiliconData said its "large language model (LLM) token spending index" fell to 97 cents on the 31st of the last month (local time). Infra & Chips.content: [## the tech buzz](/) AI Infrastructure Boom Hits Wall as Bond Yields Spike [Investment](/topics/investment)/[AI Infrastructure](/topics/ai-infrastructure) # AI Infrastructure Boom Hits Wall as Bond Yields Spike Rising Treasury yields squeeze debt-hungry data center companies funding AI buildout by [The Tech Buzz](/authors/the-tech-buzz) PUBLISHED: Sun, Sep 27, 2026, 11:35 AM UTC| UPDATED: Sun, Sep 27, 2026, 11:35 AM UTC [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) ![AI Infrastructure Boom Hits Wall as Bond Yields Spike](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto,fit=cover/https://charming-card-d91ad3487b.media.strapiapp.com/large_file_2cf1664a7a.png) The Tech Buzz may earn a commission when you buy through links on this page. This never affects which products we recommend or what we say about them. The AI infrastructure gold rush just got more expensive. As Treasury yields surge to multi-year highs, data center companies powering the artificial intelligence boom are facing a harsh new reality - the debt that's been fueling their massive expansion plans now costs significantly more. This shift threatens to slow the breakneck pace of AI infrastructure development that's been reshaping the tech landscape. The AI infrastructure boom that's been reshaping the technology landscape is running headfirst into a new obstacle: money just got a lot more expensive. Treasury yields have spiked to levels not seen in years, and that's creating serious problems for the data center companies that have been borrowing billions to build the backbone of the artificial intelligence revolution. These companies have been on an unprecedented spending spree, racing to construct massive facilities filled with [Nvidia](https://nvidia.com) GPUs and other specialized hardware needed to train and run AI models. The scale is staggering - industry estimates suggest data center operators have committed to over $200 billion in new infrastructure spending through 2027. But most of that expansion has been funded through debt, and now the bill is coming due at much higher interest rates. The timing couldn't be worse for an industry that's been operating on the assumption that cheap money would continue flowing. Major data center operators like Digital Realty Trust and Equinix have been issuing bonds at record pace to fund their AI-focused expansions. When yields were low, this strategy made perfect sense - borrow cheaply today to capture the massive revenue opportunity from AI workloads tomorrow. Advertisement But the Federal Reserve's monetary policy shift has fundamentally changed that calculus. The designs target higher compute density, tighter GPU interconnects, and data centers with hybrid or full-liquid cooling. # ASUS shows liquid-cooled Rubin systems at AI Tech 2026 in Seoul ASUS used AI Tech 2026 in Seoul to present its latest AI servers, rack systems, storage platforms, and partner technologies. The show floor centered on NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 systems and rack-scale platforms built for dense AI training and inference. The company’s [AI infrastructure portfolio](https://www.asus.com/ai/ai-infrastructure/) covers compute, storage, networking, cooling, and management. The Seoul event showed how those pieces fit into larger systems. ## Rubin NVL8 changes the GPU layout The NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 design places eight Rubin GPUs in a compact liquid-cooled section. The platform rotates the GPU orientation on the baseboard, giving the cooling system a shorter path to the heat sources. That layout lets the GPU section occupy 1U. Earlier air-cooled HGX platforms could require 6U or more for the GPU baseboard and its cooling hardware. ASUS used the saved rack space to create a second chassis segment for CPUs, SSDs, data processing units, and other system components. The result gives rack builders two cooling options. A hybrid design can combine liquid cooling for the GPUs with air cooling for other components. A full-liquid design can move more heat out of the chassis and reduce the fan capacity that the rack needs. NVIDIA also adds a new generation of NVLink Switch technology to the Rubin platform. NVLink connects GPUs inside the system, while scale-out networking links the system to other nodes. The [NVIDIA NVLink and NVLink Switch platform](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/nvlink/) provides the interconnect layer for these multi-GPU designs. ## More compute inside each GPU domain Rubin GPUs can draw more power than Hopper-generation GPUs, which raises the rack’s power and cooling requirements. ASUS positions the higher power draw alongside greater compute capacity and a larger connected memory pool. The NVL8 topology keeps more GPU-to-GPU communication inside the node. That reduces traffic across the scale-out fabric when workloads need frequent exchanges among the eight accelerators. A model can also keep more data within the local GPU domain before it needs to cross into another node. The event material supplied no independent benchmark scores, workload results, or GPU power figures. Infra & Chips.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Apple Weighs Return to Commercial Servers as Accelerator Interconnect Battle Heats Up [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Apple is evaluating a return to the commercial server market, with a proposed product targeting AI inference workloads, built on its in-house M-series chips, and potentially incorporating Nvidia's NVLink Fusion interconnect technology. The move comes as the accelerator interconnect market undergoes rapid expansion: IDC data shows global data center Ethernet switch revenue grew 64.5% year-over-year in Q2 2026, while Dell'Oro reports that AI backend network switch sales surpassed frontend network sales for the first time. Interconnect suppliers are disclosing progress at a rapid clip—Cadence has validated UALink solutions on TSMC's N3P process, while Cornelis and Delos Data have secured substantial funding and unveiled product roadmaps. Apple's chip technology expertise underpins its potential entry: TechInsights' independent teardown analysis of the A20 Pro confirms TSMC's 2nm process performance claims, and Apple has locked in the vast majority of TSMC's 2026 2nm capacity. The choice of interconnect architecture will be deeply intertwined with its in-house chip roadmap, emerging as a decisive factor in next-generation server competitiveness. ##### Key Elements ![Apple Weighs Return to Commercial Servers as Accelerator Interconnect Battle Heats Up](https://img.biggo.com/1hWV_lTfy6T6zMYeWM4jBMt9j-n6Q7dUaFpnCG5Fi0c/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA5LzMzZmIwNDE4LTRjZGUtNDdkOS05YzVkLTJlNjZhZDNjYmY1NV8xNzkwNTU5NjA2X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Apple is evaluating a return to the commercial server market, with a proposed product targeting AI inference workloads, built on its in-house M-series chips, and potentially incorporating Nvidia's NVLink Fusion interconnect technology. The move comes at a pivotal moment when the accelerator interconnect market is expanding rapidly and multiple suppliers are disclosing product progress at an accelerating pace—the choice of server interconnect architecture is becoming a core variable shaping next-generation data center architecture. According to industry publication EE Times China, Apple has already deployed its in-house chips in private cloud computing infrastructure to handle Apple Intelligence's cloud inference tasks. But if the company were to sell servers to external customers, those products would enter third-party data centers and must integrate deeply with customers' existing networking, software, and operations frameworks. For a company with chip design capabilities, commercial servers remain a complex business requiring the orchestration of an external supply chain. Entering the server market with in-house silicon first requires settling on an interconnect architecture, then finding partners who can supply interfaces, switching, and connector components. Over the past two weeks, interconnect supply chain vendors have disclosed interface validations, product roadmaps, and sampling plans in rapid succession—competition around this procurement decision has visibly intensified. On September 23, electronic design automation company Cadence announced it had demonstrated UALink solutions on TSMC's (2330.TW) N3P process node, providing silicon-validated interface designs for chip companies adopting open interconnect standards. The same day, networking chip company Cornelis further detailed its product roadmap for next-generation AI systems, planning to offload certain data processing tasks to network interface cards and switch chips. Market data confirms the explosive growth in this segment.
